reference.source: Auerbach's Wilderness Medicine / Bove and Davis' Diving Medicine
clinicalPearls: An umbrella term encompassing decompression sickness, from bubbles forming out of dissolved inert gas, and arterial gas embolism, from pulmonary barotrauma driving gas into the arterial circulation
Decompression sickness ranges from musculoskeletal joint pain (the bends) and a mottled skin rash (cutis marmorata), to serious neurological forms with spinal cord or cerebral involvement
Arterial gas embolism typically presents dramatically within minutes of surfacing, with stroke-like deficits, loss of consciousness, or seizure
Symptoms usually begin during or within hours of surfacing; any neurological complaint after diving should be treated as decompression illness until proven otherwise
Definitive treatment is recompression in a hyperbaric chamber with hyperbaric oxygen, alongside high-flow surface oxygen, lying flat, and fluids during transfer
Flying after diving too soon reduces ambient pressure further and can precipitate or worsen decompression illness, so recommended pre-flight surface intervals must be observed
The dive profile, including depth, bottom time, ascent rate, and any missed decompression stops, is central to assessing risk
A patent foramen ovale increases the risk of paradoxical bubble embolisation in some divers
reference.pathophysiology: Decompression illness has two overlapping mechanisms. In decompression sickness, inert gas (usually nitrogen) that dissolved into tissues under pressure comes out of solution as bubbles when ambient pressure falls too quickly on ascent; these bubbles obstruct vessels, distort tissue, and trigger inflammatory and clotting cascades, causing joint pain, skin mottling (cutis marmorata), and neurological injury, particularly of the spinal cord. In arterial gas embolism, over-expansion of the lungs on ascent (pulmonary barotrauma) forces gas into the pulmonary veins and systemic arteries, embolising to the brain and producing acute stroke-like features. Reducing ambient pressure further, as with flying soon after diving, exacerbates bubble formation.
additionalDifferentials: Stroke or transient ischaemic attack from another cause
Marine envenomation or other diving-related injury
additionalInvestigations: Detailed dive profile review including depth, bottom time, ascent rate, and decompression stops
Full neurological examination to detect spinal cord and cerebral involvement
Skin examination for cutis marmorata and joint assessment for the bends
Assessment of oxygenation and cardiorespiratory status
Investigation for a patent foramen ovale (e.g. bubble contrast echocardiography) in appropriate cases
Consultation with a diving medicine or hyperbaric service to guide recompression
redFlags: Neurological deficit, altered consciousness, or seizure after diving
Rapid stroke-like onset within minutes of surfacing, suggesting arterial gas embolism
Respiratory distress or chest pain suggesting pulmonary barotrauma
Rapidly progressing symptoms or a history of missed decompression stops or rapid ascent
Cutis marmorata, which may herald more serious decompression sickness
reference.prognosis: Prompt recompression and hyperbaric oxygen give many patients a good or full recovery, but delay in treatment, severe neurological (especially spinal) involvement, or arterial gas embolism can leave lasting deficits; early recognition and surface oxygen substantially improve outcomes.
pitfalls: Dismissing joint pain or vague post-dive symptoms and delaying recompression
Failing to give high-flow surface oxygen while arranging transfer
Allowing the patient to fly too soon after diving, worsening the illness
Overlooking arterial gas embolism when stroke-like symptoms follow surfacing
Not considering a patent foramen ovale in unexplained or recurrent cases
management: Give high-flow surface oxygen immediately and lie the patient flat while arranging transfer
Provide fluid resuscitation, oral or intravenous, to counter haemoconcentration
Arrange urgent recompression in a hyperbaric chamber with hyperbaric oxygen as the definitive treatment
Consult a diving medicine or hyperbaric service early to guide management and transfer
Treat arterial gas embolism as a time-critical emergency with the same measures, recognising its stroke-like presentation within minutes of surfacing
Avoid any further reduction in ambient pressure, not permitting flying until cleared, and investigate for a patent foramen ovale in appropriate cases
Review the dive profile and counsel on safe ascent practice and adequate pre-flight surface intervals to prevent recurrence
